To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the visual pigments of most tropical marine fishes are retinal-1, and that the spectral position of these retinal-1s does not correlate with the activity patterns of the species.

(1) the visual pigments of tropical reef fishes are retinal-1, and their λmax are tightly grouped between 490 and 502 nm, (2) the spectral position of these rhodopsins does not correlate with the diurnal or noctural activity of their species, (3) the deeper-living fishes have rhodopsin with λmax at the shorter wavelengths, and (4) the spectral distribution of light at twilight narrows and shifts toward shorter wavelengths, which
the rhodopsin of a fish is spectrally matched to its environment and, as a consequence, predation is kept in check during the “Quiet Time” that occurs at dusk.

the relationships between light and visual pigments, and how these are related to behavior, in a natural environment.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the visual pigments of tropical marine fishes are adapted to the spectral quality of the underwater light, as modified by the atmosphere during twilight.
the visual pigments of tropical marine fishes are tuned to match the spectral quality of twilight light.
the rhodopsin of tropical marine fishes is an excellent match for the light available at twilight, and that this match provides a visual advantage for both prey and predator.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the spectral position of rhodopsin in tropical marine fishes is determined by the light environment, and that the spectral distributions of light and visual pigments in these fishes are related to behavior and photoreception.
visual sensitivity is optimized by a matching between the spectral distribution of background light, the spectral distribution of the visual pigments and the visual requirements of the animals.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the spectral position of the rhodopsin is not a random event.
the visual pigments of tropical marine fishes are not adapted to the diurnal and nocturnal habits of the animals.
the visual pigments of reef fishes are not adapted to the light available during daytime, but rather to the light available in the twilight periods.
